extracted.intended_audience: agency lawyers, regulators, administrative law scholars, and policymakers interested in AI use in rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Minimum administrative-law standards for how U.S. agencies may use AI (especially LLMs) in rulemaking and notice-and-comment procedures, focusing on required human involvement, justification of methods, and protection against procedural failings under the APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive human involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must provide substantive human involvement in the rulemaking process and may not entirely outsource rulemaking to AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The APA and its case law are plausibly read to require certain forms of substantive human involvement in rulemaking, which would preclude agencies from entirely outsourcing their work to AI. The piece contrasts full outsourcing (a 'rubber-stamping' model) with meaningful human deliberation and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain and justify methodological choice to use AI
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency relies on AI, it must explain and justify that methodological choice to satisfy administrative-law reasoned-decisionmaking requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies bear an 'affirmative burden' to 'explain the assumptions and methodology used in preparing' any model and 'provide a full analytical defense' of challenged aspects. Rubber-stamping the output of a tool known to be prone to error without this explanation would be arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain assumptions, model development, prompting, and validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must reasonably explain how they chose and developed the model, how they prompted it, how they validated its outputs, and why they view those results as reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically: describe model choice and development, the prompting/design choices, validation procedures for outputs, and the agency's basis for treating the outputs as reliable. This mirrors longstanding requirements when agencies use mathematical models to inform rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be conscious of model limits (hallucinations, sycophancy, bias, context windows)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must be conscious of and account for the known limitations and failure modes of LLMs, including hallucinations, sycophancy, propagation of biases, and limited context windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes LLMs 'hallucinate' false information, may act 'sycophantically', replicate biases in training data, and have limited 'context windows' that impair processing long documents—important concerns for rulemaking. Agencies must account for these limits when relying on AI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoned decisionmaking: examine relevant data and articulate satisfactory explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency action must rest on examination of relevant data, an articulated satisfactory explanation, and consideration of relevant factors; grounds must be 'clearly disclosed and adequately sustained.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites APA requirements and Supreme Court/D.C. Circuit formulations: agencies must 'examine the relevant data,' 'articulate a satisfactory explanation,' and base decisions 'on a consideration of the relevant factors.' AI use cannot short-circuit those obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rubber-stamping; ensure meaningful human deliberation and review
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may not merely rubber-stamp AI outputs; they must meaningfully deliberate and undertake substantive human review before adopting AI-generated proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post uses examples (e.g., DOGE's proposal allocating 12 minutes for human review or .01 seconds per comment) to illustrate inadequate review. An agency that simply rubber-stamps an LLM-chosen course of action risks being found to have abdicated its duties and offered 'contrived' reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately consider and address significant public comments
rubrics_metrics.description: When using AI in notice-and-comment proceedings, agencies must consider and address significant public comments and cannot rely on severely skewed automated summaries or responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: D.C. Circuit precedent warns that dependence on 'severely skewed staff summaries' may breach the duty to accord consideration to comments. LLMs may generate 'severely skewed' assessments; agencies must ensure independent human effort to review and consider comments and to respond appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and justify comment-processing workflows involving AI
rubrics_metrics.description: If AI is used to sort, categorize, summarize, or respond to public comments, agencies must document how the AI was used and justify that the resulting processing preserves meaningful consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes EPA's plan to 'use artificial intelligence to help sort and categorize public comments' but states 'human supervision and input are still required throughout comment processing.' Agencies should document supervision and how AI-assisted workflows preserve legal obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prejudgment and closed-mindedness induced by AI prompting
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies and decisionmakers must avoid prejudging matters; they must not adopt AI-generated lines of reasoning that close off genuine reconsideration or simulate an 'unalterably closed mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due-process disqualification requires a 'clear and convincing showing' of an unalterably closed mind, but AI prompting and sycophancy may make a system or process literally incapable of challenging prompt premises. Agencies must guard against processes that lock in a predetermined outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency retains ultimate responsibility; human accountability as safety valve
rubrics_metrics.description: Ultimate responsibility for policy decisions must remain with the agency rather than the computer; human actors must retain final decision authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The D.C. Circuit has described an insistence that 'ultimate responsibility for the policy decision remains with the agency rather than the computer' as a 'safety valve' when sophisticated methodology is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize increased exposure to arbitrary-and-capricious challenge when relying on AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should recognize that reliance on AI increases exposure to arbitrary-and-capricious claims if AI outputs misstate, disregard, or are implausible relative to agency records and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post ties LLM failure modes to State Farm categories (e.g., reliance on improper factors, failure to consider important aspects, explanations counter to evidence). Agencies must guard against those failure modes when integrating AI into decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat these standards as a floor, not a ceiling
rubrics_metrics.description: The minimum standards outlined should be understood as a floor; additional legal and policy safeguards may be appropriate depending on deployment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note that substantive human involvement is a minimum and not necessarily the full set of safeguards that ought to govern agency AI usage; more stringent oversight, regulation, or legislation may be necessary.
